Q22009876.summary: The Mother of God sits on a high throne holding the Christ Child, who blesses, while Saints Anthony and Theodosius, founders of the Kyiv Monastery of the Caves, stand at either side with unfurled scrolls. It is the earliest surviving image of these two founding monks. The Christ Child, held at the centre of the composition, shows that the monks' prayers are offered to the incarnate Lord.
facts: Saint Anthony's scroll carries a monastic exhortation, rendered in the Russian Wikipedia article as 'I pray you, children: let us keep to abstinence and not be idle, for we have the Lord as our helper.'
Tradition holds that in 1288 Prince Roman of Bryansk was healed of blindness before this icon and founded the Svensky Monastery, where it stayed until 1925; it is now in the Tretyakov Gallery.
Q22009876.notes: Dating is disputed. The Commons description (citing the Tretyakov Gallery) gives c. 1288; some scholars (e.g. Konrad Onasch, per French Wikipedia) and the traditional attribution to Alypius place it in the 11th–12th century. Wikidata records both. Corrected to c. 1288, which moves it out of this batch's centuries.

Q80079053.summary: On the face of this gold coin Christ appears as a bust, his right hand raised in blessing and his left holding a jewelled Gospel book, with the arms of a cross behind his head. He is shown with short, tightly curled hair and a close beard, a distinctive type used on the coins of Justinian II's second reign. The Latin legend names him 'Jesus Christ, King of those who reign', placing the emperor, shown on the reverse, beneath the true Lord.
facts: Justinian II was the first Byzantine emperor to put the image of Christ on coins issued in his name.
The Cleveland Museum of Art records the obverse inscription as dN IhS ChS REX REGNANTIUM, with the bust of Justinian II holding a cross and a globe inscribed PAX on the reverse.

The short-haired, curly Christ seen here differs from the long-haired type of Justinian's first reign; Wikipedia's article on Santa Maria Antiqua notes that this coin type may have influenced painters in Rome.
Q80079053.notes: Dated 705 by the museum (start of Justinian II's second reign, 705–711).

cur:catacombs-lazarus-peter-fragment-314.summary: At the left of this fragment, the young Christ, holding a scroll, reaches towards the swaddled Lazarus standing in his temple-like tomb, while Martha kneels at his feet; to the right, soldiers lead Peter away under arrest and a cock recalls his denial. The carving is crisp and expressive, the faces individualised.
facts: The museum describes the scenes as the raising of Lazarus, the arrest of Peter, and an orans reworked as the denial of Peter.
The small cockerel at the lower right alludes to Christ's prophecy of Peter's denial.

cur:catacombs-arles-traditio-legis.summary: Five arched niches frame the scenes; at the centre Christ stands on the hill of paradise with its four rivers and hands the unrolled scroll of the Law to Peter, while Paul acclaims him. Other niches show further biblical scenes with the apostles. The Traditio Legis presents Christ as the lawgiver of the new covenant.
facts: Commons records that it comes from the Alyscamps cemetery of Arles and is carved from Carrara marble (FAN.92.00.2487).
A second Commons photograph of the same sarcophagus (Arles sarcophagus with christ.jpg) shows it from a different angle.

wga:zearly/1/4mosaics/2ravenna/4nuovo/5t.summary: Following the ancient custom of dining, Christ and the twelve apostles recline around a semicircular table. Christ, haloed and robed in purple, lies at the place of honour on the left, while the apostles crowd in a tight arc behind a white cloth set with loaves and a large dish holding two fish. Rather than the moment of the bread and cup, the mosaic shows the company gathered at table, a memorable early image of the Supper on the eve of the Passion.
facts: The Passion scenes on the upper south wall correspond to the Gospel passages read aloud in the church during Lent under Theodoric.
The narrative panels were executed by at least two artists, and the mosaics were renovated and altered in the mid-19th century by Felice Kibel.
